title: Pointers: Talking About Where Something Is

questions.question: What does a pointer actually hold?
options: The address of some object, that is, where it lives in memory
A copy of the object it refers to
The size of the object it refers to
A reference count for the object
questions.explanation: A pointer is a variable holding an address. It says where something is, and nothing about how long it will stay there.

questions.question: In an expression, what does the star in *p mean?
options: The value living at the address p holds
The address of p
Multiplication by p
That p may be null
questions.explanation: In a type, the star means pointer to. In an expression it dereferences, giving the object at that address. The same symbol doing two jobs is a genuine wart.

questions.question: Why return nullptr rather than an index of minus one for not found?
options: nullptr is a value the language itself understands as nothing, so it needs no convention
Because indexes cannot be negative
Because pointers are faster than integers
Because minus one is a valid index in C++
questions.explanation: Every codebase invents a different sentinel index and somebody eventually forgets to check it. nullptr means nothing found in a way the compiler and the reader both recognise.

questions.question: Why does the reference guard against a null array before looping?
options: Reading through a null pointer is undefined behaviour, and a null array with a positive count is a caller mistake
Because looping over zero elements is a compile error
To make the function faster
Because the count might overflow
questions.explanation: A function that is handed nonsense should answer honestly rather than read memory it was never given. Guarding costs one comparison.

questions.question: What is the one rule that makes pointers safe?
options: A pointer is only as valid as the thing it points at
A pointer must always be const
A pointer must never be null
A pointer must always be freed
questions.explanation: An address keeps nothing alive. Whenever you hold a pointer you must be able to say what keeps its target alive and for how long.

questions.question: When is a raw pointer still the right tool in modern C++?
options: Talking to hardware or C libraries, and referring to something that obviously outlives the reference
Whenever you want to avoid copying a large object
Whenever a value might be missing
Whenever you allocate memory
questions.explanation: For avoiding copies use a reference, for a possibly missing value use std::optional, and for ownership use the types in lesson 02-04. Raw pointers keep the two roles listed.
